This piece ignores one of the biggest reasons there are more people in custody awaiting trial: criminal cases are taking longer to get to trial, because judges will almost always grant a defendant's request for a continuance. Interestingly, Ms. McDannel bears part of the blame for this herself. In 2009, while representing a person named Kalani Maalona, Ms. McDannel did no work to prepare for a hearing - in fact, she sent another lawyer from her office to ask for a continuance. Judge Phillip Volland denied the request, and the case went forward. Mr. Maalona appealed and the Court of Appeals reversed. Judges have learned their lesson and will give allow defendants to delays their cases for years. Ending the culture of continuances is the real way to address criminal justice spending - not that you'll hear a defense attorney say so.

I wonder if Brown or any of the commentators below know that once electricity is generated, it cannot be stored. It's not like there is a bin of electricity waiting to be sold or an inventory of electricity. It's produced and consumed instantly and any excess demand must be met by buying electricity and any excess supply sold - all done immediately at whatever the price is on the trading market by the independent system operator to maintain system balance. If this wasn't done, you would see brownouts and energy spikes constantly. The nature of the market means that spot prices are incredibly volatile. And remember that generation cannot be spun up instantaneously - whereas demand can come on and off at any time. There is a lot to criticize Ontario for on the electricity side, but Brown making an issue of this one day's trading is kind of sleazy (unless he truly does not know better) and relies upon total ignorance about the trading market to succeed.

Like Rick - I think stop loss orders rarely provide the protection people think they do. In fact I consider them to be counterproductive. Primarily because if you are concerned about the value of a particular stock you probably should be selling now and not waiting for the price to start going down. Using a broad portfolio stop-loss with a 7 or 8% tolerance in theory sounds great but rarely works as intended. Inevitably you end up selling good companies that you really didn't want to sell because of a temporary price bump. Worse yet you get the scenario of 2008 and your order can't get filled at the 8% mark and you end up selling well under that point. To make matters worse in the case of a broad portfolio disposition if the stocks held are in a cash account and were bought years ago you could trigger substantial capital gains tax that ordinarily would have been deferred well into the future. Leaving you with even less to take advantage of a market recovery.
